title: How Midnight Regulations Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain midnight regulations: last-minute rules a outgoing president pushes through during the transition period before leaving office. They cover the transition and the Bush-era W-removed-keyboard anecdote, the Federal Register and the surge in pages, how regulations are created through agencies and reviewed by OIRA, the 60-day window that makes rules hard to undo, the Congressional Review Act and its limits, Clinton's high volume of midnight rules, Bush's suspension of the arsenic rule, examples of contested EPA and healthcare rules, and proposed reforms. The episode closes with listener mail corrections (Tourette's vs. OCD, Dutch word for farm) and a haiku from a listener.
topics: OIRA Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs

segments.title: Opening banter and setup
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on midnight regulations and banter briefly before describing a presidential transition, including the anecdote of the W key removed from White House keyboards when the Bush team arrived.

segments.title: What midnight regulations are
segments.summary: Definition of the midnight period, from the November election to inauguration. Outgoing presidents push rules through, sometimes to extend influence or hamstring the successor. Clinton's roughly 26,000 pages of new regulations are cited.

segments.title: Federal Register evidence and ProPublica list
segments.summary: Political scientists studied Federal Register page volume and found it rises sharply in midnight periods. The hosts recommend ProPublica's list tracking Bush-era midnight regulations.

segments.title: How regulations are created and why they affect everyday life
segments.summary: Congress creates agencies, and the executive branch carries out mandates through regulations. Examples include EPA emissions testing, FDA, SEC, and FCC profanity rules. Regulatory agencies are where government touches the public.

segments.title: OIRA review and the 60-day window
segments.summary: The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs reviews proposed rules, including cost-benefit analysis. Rules become law after 30 or 60 days, and the 60-day window lets outgoing presidents finish rules before successors take office, making them hard to undo.
topics: OIRA Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs

segments.title: Repealing rules and the Congressional Review Act
segments.summary: Repealing a rule requires studies and alternatives. The Congressional Review Act, signed by Clinton, lets Congress repeal rules by simple majority but still needs presidential signature, so it works only when the president and Congress share a party. It was used once, in 2001, against an ergonomics rule. Staffing shortages and mass public comments are discussed. Reform ideas such as barring new rules in the midnight period are mentioned.

segments.title: Bush's midnight regulation fights and contested rules
segments.summary: Bush's chief of staff reportedly set a June 1 deadline for agency submissions. Bush suspended Clinton's arsenic water rule, later reversed. Examples discussed include EPA power plant pollution controls, fisheries science, financial planner conflict-of-interest disclosure, the right to conscience rule on contraception and abortion, and oil drilling in polar bear habitat.

segments.title: Listener mail: corrections and haiku
segments.summary: Corrections: Chris Jackson had Tourette's rather than OCD, and a Dutch listener notes that the Dutch word for farm is not boerderij as implied. A listener, Devin Wallace, receives a haiku reading.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts point listeners to the website for more on Tourette's and sign off.
